column1: Linguistics|broad_field|idea|linguistics|§1.3, descriptive and prescriptive approaches|Investigate language through systematic observations rather than treating preferred usage as an empirical rule.|local:authored:000132|Same science-of-language identity and descriptive approach already present in earlier cards.|

Phonology|topic|idea|phonemes|§4.1, The essence of phonology|Study how a language organizes and combines sound or sign units beyond their physical production.|Q40998|Same systematic-organization field; the source also notes signed-language patterns.|

Morphology|topic|idea|morphology|§5.1, opening examples and morpheme definition|Analyze how form-and-meaning units combine into words, including words expressing sentence-like meanings.|Q38311|Same linguistic word-structure sense, separate from biological or archaeological morphology.|

Minimal pair|idea|idea|minimalpair|§4.3, Comparing distributions with minimal pairs|Use a one-position contrast between otherwise matching words as evidence that two sounds distinguish meanings.|local:catalog:minimal-pair|Same phonemic-evidence method as the prior candidate; preserve canonical ID.|

Allophone|idea|idea|phonemes|§4.1, The phonological units of spoken language|Recognize physically different pronunciations treated as realizations of a single abstract phoneme.|local:catalog:allophone|Same noncontrastive pronunciation-variant identity as the baseline.|

Complementary distribution|idea|idea|complementary|§4.4, Phones without contrastive distribution; Phonetic similarity|Recognize nonoverlapping sound environments without assuming this alone proves that the sounds share one phoneme.|local:catalog:allophone|A distributional relation provides evidence about allophones but does not itself identify a single phoneme.|

Allomorph|idea|idea|allomorphy|§5.4, opening definition and plural examples|Recognize different forms of one morpheme, with variants conditioned by sounds or specific lexical roots.|local:catalog:allomorph|Allomorphy is the variation phenomenon already represented by the Allomorph identity; reuse it.|Allomorphy

Reduplication|idea|idea|reduplication|§5.3, Reduplication|Repeat all or part of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast.|Q38311|A specific word-formation mechanism differs from the general morphology field.|

Constituency tests|idea|idea|constituency|§6.4, introduction; Replacement Test; Movement Test|Combine replacement and movement evidence to identify word groups that behave as sentence units.|local:catalog:constituency-tests|Same multi-test syntax method as the existing candidate; preserve ID.|Constituency test

Structural ambiguity|idea|idea|ambiguity|§6.17, telescope example|Derive different interpretations from alternative phrase attachments while keeping the words unchanged.|local:catalog:structural-ambiguity|Same syntactic-attachment distinction already represented in the baseline.|

Semantic compositionality|idea|idea|composition|§7.2, definition and complex-word example|Explain how a novel expression's meaning depends on its parts and how those parts are combined.|local:authored:000132|A specific account of meaning combination is distinct from the field of linguistics and musical composition.|Compositionality

Semantic entailment|idea|idea|entailment|§7.3, Entailments|Test whether one sentence being true necessarily makes another true by looking for contradiction under denial.|Q1076131|Entailment is truth-preservation; presupposition is background information an utterance takes for granted.|Entailment

Conversational implicature|idea|idea|entailment|§7.3, Implicatures|Distinguish a contextually suggested conclusion from a necessary implication by checking whether it can be cancelled.|Q1076131|Cancellable suggestions differ from presupposed background assumptions and semantic entailments.|Implicature

Presupposition|idea|idea|entailment|§7.3, Presuppositions|Recognize information an utterance presents as already accepted, such as prior activity implied by stopping it.|Q1076131|Same assumed-background-context sense; retain registered ID.|

International Phonetic Alphabet|topic|named_subject|ipa|§3.6, Transcription; The International Phonetic Alphabet|Use a cross-language sound notation to avoid inconsistencies between ordinary spelling and pronunciation.|Q21204|Same named standardized notation system in the inventory; retain canonical ID.|IPA

Historical linguistics|broad_field|idea|languagechange|§10.3, Language changes|Track changes through competing variants rather than treating a language as fixed across generations.|Q190375|Same study-of-language-change field; source distinguishes change from stable variation.|

Variationist sociolinguistics|topic|idea|variationist|§10.1, opening explanation|Analyze how linguistic and social conditions alter the probability of variants in language as actually used.|local:authored:000132|This empirical approach is narrower than linguistics and differs from an idealized grammar alone.|

Sociolinguistic interview|idea|idea|variationmethods|§10.5, Sociolinguistic interviews and corpora|Compare speech across tasks that elicit different levels of self-monitoring, or collect natural conversation.|Q772835|A defined data-collection method differs from the broad study of language and social life.|

Observer's paradox in sociolinguistics|idea|idea|variationmethods|§10.5, Sociolinguistic interviews and corpora|Recognize that systematically recording everyday speech may change the very speech researchers want to observe.|Q772835|A methodological tension in observation is distinct from linguistic anthropology generally and from logical paradoxes.|Observer's paradox

Principle of accountability in sociolinguistics|idea|idea|variationmethods|§10.5, Quantitative analysis|Count every eligible variant to form a denominator instead of counting only the interesting pronunciation.|local:authored:000132|This denominator rule for variation analysis is a specific method, not accountability in governance.|Principle of accountability

Sociolinguistic corpus|idea|idea|variationmethods|§10.5, Sociolinguistic interviews and corpora|Combine recordings across a relevant speaker sample so community patterns can be distinguished from individual habits.|local:authored:000132|A structured empirical collection is distinct from the research field and from one interview.|

Style shifting|idea|idea|socialstatus|§10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading|Observe speakers changing variant frequencies with speaking context rather than assigning one fixed style to each class.|local:authored:000132|Within-speaker contextual variation differs from general language structure or artistic style.|

Linguistic change from above|idea|idea|languagechange|§10.3, Changes from above|Trace consciously noticed adoption of a prestigious outside variant, illustrated by New York City's rhoticity shift.|Q190375|A socially conscious route of language change is narrower than historical linguistics.|Change from above

Linguistic change from below|idea|idea|languagechange|§10.3, Changes from below|Trace language-system changes that spread below conscious social awareness, such as gradual vowel fronting.|Q190375|An unselfconscious route of change differs from prestigious conscious adoption and from the broad historical field.|Change from below

Atlas linguistique de la France|topic|named_subject|variationmethods|§10.5, Dialectology: Then and now|See how mapped transcriptions from many places make regional language variation inspectable.|Q190375|The particular survey atlas is a named research work, not historical linguistics generally.|Linguistic Atlas of France

Fangyan|topic|named_subject|variationmethods|§10.5, Dialectology: Then and now, Yang Xiong paragraph|Explore how a Han-era collection of regional words preserves evidence used to infer earlier dialect groupings.|Q190375|The specific regional-vocabulary work is distinct from the general history-of-language field.|Fāngyán;方言

William Labov|topic|named_subject|socialstatus|§10.7, 1966 Lower East Side study|See how occupation, education, and income were used to compare linguistic variant frequencies across social strata.|local:authored:000132|The researcher and documented study design are a named learning subject, not the broad field.|

Chantale Cenerini|topic|named_subject|michif|§9.7, interview on local context and community stories|Learn from her account of documenting community stories while respecting distinct local Michif and Métis language histories.|local:authored:000133|A particular scholar's community-grounded practice differs from the general revitalization activity.|

Language documentation|topic|idea|michif|§9.7, story-documentation and family-legacy discussion|Create records of language use and community knowledge that can serve both research and family legacies.|local:authored:000133|Documentation preserves records; baseline revitalization concerns continued use and intergenerational transmission.|

Community-led language reclamation|facet_or_application|idea|michif|§9.7, community-specific histories and priorities|Let communities' own language histories and goals guide locally tailored reclamation work rather than assuming one shared language.|local:authored:000133|A governance and locality facet of revitalization is separately supported, not a second name for its general goal.|

Peer learning|topic|idea|peerpaper|§II, Overview of Peer Instruction|Develop understanding by explaining reasoning to other learners and considering their explanations.|local:authored:000137|Same general collaborative-learning meaning; peer instruction supplies a specific example.|

Testing effect|idea|idea|ies|Recommendation 5b, printed pp. 21–22|Use effortful recall with corrective feedback as a learning activity rather than treating quizzes only as measurement.|Q7705913|Same general benefit of testing studied material as the baseline Testing effect; instructional phrasing alone is not a separate identity.|Retrieval practice;Practice testing

Spacing effect|idea|idea|ies|Recommendation 1, printed pp. 5–8|Separate encounters with course material over time while keeping total study time comparable.|Q1095859|Same general spacing benefit as the preserved baseline meaning; instructional wording does not create a new identity.|Spaced practice;Distributed practice

Interleaved practice|idea|idea|interleavestudy|Structured Abstract, Intervention and Control Condition|Mix different mathematical problem types so learners must select a strategy instead of repeating one blocked routine.|Q133500|Mixing task types is distinct from temporal spacing and from alternating worked examples with unsolved problems.|Interleaving

Worked example|idea|idea|ies|Recommendation 2, printed pp. 9–10|Study a demonstrated solution path before attempting comparable problems, especially while building initial expertise.|Q133500|A fully shown solution is a specific instructional representation, not learning generally.|

Faded worked examples|facet_or_application|idea|ies|Recommendation 2, printed p. 10|Gradually remove later solution steps so learners supply more of the solution as expertise develops.|Q133500|The progressive withdrawal of guidance is distinct from providing a complete worked solution.|

Coordinating graphics and verbal explanations|facet_or_application|idea|ies|Recommendation 3, printed pp. 13–14|Place relevant verbal explanations alongside the visual elements they explain so learners can connect representations.|Q8434|This is an instructional coordination technique, not a claim about fixed visual or verbal learning styles.|

Connecting concrete and abstract representations|facet_or_application|idea|ies|Recommendation 4, printed pp. 15–17|Explicitly map familiar objects or examples onto abstract symbols so knowledge can transfer beyond surface features.|Q18205125|The baseline is a philosophical distinction between abstract and concrete; this is a teaching application linking representations.|

Prequestioning|facet_or_application|idea|ies|Recommendation 5a, printed pp. 19–20|Ask questions before exposure to focus study, while preserving attention to material the questions do not cover.|Q133500|A pre-exposure instructional tactic differs from retrieval of previously studied content; the guide rates its evidence low.|

Delayed judgments of learning|facet_or_application|idea|ies|Recommendation 6a, printed pp. 23–24|After a delay, use only a cue to judge future recall so immediate familiarity is less misleading.|Q1602656|A specific cue-only calibration procedure is narrower than general self-assessment; the guide notes classroom-evidence limits.|

Self-explanation|idea|idea|ies|Recommendation 7; checklist, printed p. 4|Generate one's own causal or logical explanations during study rather than merely repeating the presented answer.|Q133500|An active explanation-generation method is distinct from general learning and from answering for assessment.|

Formative assessment|idea|idea|formative|Formative assessment; final paragraph|Use evidence during learning to adjust teaching and study, with purpose mattering more than a test's format.|Q27318|A formative use of evidence differs from the broad assessment instrument and summative evaluation.|

Mastery learning|idea|idea|mastery|What is it?; distinction from teaching for mastery|Hold learning goals steady while varying time and corrective support before progression to new units.|Q133500|An instructional progression model differs from general learning and from merely aiming for deep understanding.|

Eric Mazur|topic|named_subject|peerpaper|Title and author affiliations; §II|Explore how a physicist's course redesign made individual commitments and peer reasoning part of lectures.|local:authored:000137|A specific educator-researcher and his documented course redesign differ from the general peer-learning activity.|

Peer Instruction|idea|idea|peerpaper|§II, Overview of Peer Instruction|Sequence an individual conceptual answer, peer explanation, a second vote, and instructor feedback during class.|local:authored:000137|A defined classroom protocol is narrower than general peer learning.|Peer instruction
